title: Introduction to Business Administration (BA-A), Prof. Dr. Marvin Hanisch
info: **Exam:** two-part, digital, on-campus written exam on **26 January**: **180 minutes, 180 points, 100 % of the grade**. Lecture part: closed-ended questions on core learning objectives. Tutorial part: case-based (unfamiliar company), 5 tasks along the content blocks.
- **Content areas:** organizing (why do firms exist?), strategy (capture value), innovation (create value), marketing (deliver value), supply chain (orchestrate value), integration.
- **Exercise classes:** PBL cases (N26, L'Oréal, Weisse Arena, Appenzeller) and touchpoints on the running case ON (submissions due Tuesdays 23:59 on Canvas).
- **Textbook among your PDFs:** Bieger, Heer, Kuster & Tuckermann (2021), *An Introduction to Management Studies* (St. Gallen Management Model).
- Your PDFs cover Lectures **1–4** (organizing and strategy). Innovation, marketing, SCM and integration will appear once you add their slides.

questions.question: Explain the make-or-buy decision with transaction cost economics: why do firms exist (Coase), what costs arise on the market and in the hierarchy, and how does Williamson's graph add the hybrid option?
questions.model: Coase (1937): every transaction has costs (initiation, negotiation, execution, monitoring, adjustment); if these market costs exceed the costs of organizing internally, the transaction is carried out in the firm → firms exist because the market is not free to use. Hierarchy costs: internal coordination, inefficiency from lacking competitive pressure, risk taking: higher at low complexity but rising more slowly. Market costs are low for simple transactions but rise quickly with scale, scope and complexity → make when beyond the intersection. Williamson (1985): along asset specificity, the market is cheapest at low specificity, hybrids (alliances, cost of cooperation) at medium, hierarchy at high specificity (hold-up risk).

keyPoints.text: Coase: transaction costs make the market costly → firms exist
Graph logic: hierarchy starts higher, rises more slowly → make beyond the intersection
Williamson: market / hybrid / hierarchy along asset specificity

questions.question: A ride-hailing app enters a city's taxi market. Using the Five Forces, assess the threat of new entry and the threat of substitution for traditional taxi firms, and explain what this means for the taxi industry's profitability.
questions.model: Threat of new entry: high, because capital requirements are low (an app instead of a company-owned fleet), passengers face low switching costs (just switch apps), and virtually no proprietary technology is required (lecture: Uber vs. MyTaxi/Free Now). Threat of substitution: e.g. car-sharing, public transport or ride-hailing as a different way to meet the mobility need; high when the substitute offers good value for money and switching costs are low. Strong forces mean weak industry profitability: the more these forces press, the less value incumbents can capture (Porter: profitability is highest when forces are weak).

keyPoints.text: Threat of entry high, with at least two determinants from the lecture
Threat of substitution assessed with determinants (value for money, switching costs)
Conclusion: strong forces → lower profitability (Porter logic)
